How much flood risk is here?

FEMA's National Risk Index rates Jefferson County's coastal flood risk Relatively Moderate and inland flood risk Relatively Moderate, from expected annual loss.

  • Coastal flood riskRelatively Moderate
  • Coastal modeled annual loss (county)$1,465,971/yr (Relatively Moderate, 74th national percentile)
  • Inland flood riskRelatively Moderate
  • Inland modeled annual loss (county)$31,824,259/yr (Relatively Moderate, 15th national percentile)

Modeled annual loss is FEMA's estimate for the whole county (all buildings), not any one home's expected loss or premium, and not a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Am I required to carry it?

About 16.1% of the NFIP policy units in this dataset for Jefferson County are in mapped high-risk (A/V) zones — not 16.1% of all buildings. In a Special Flood Hazard Area a federally backed mortgage legally requires flood insurance.

  • Zone X9,414 policy units
  • Zone B5,349 policy units
  • Zone C2,703 policy units
  • Zone AH1,469 policy units
  • Zone AE978 policy units
  • Zone A450 policy units
  • Zone AHB155 policy units
  • Zone A15123 policy units
  • Other or unclassified zones183 policy units

Zone mix by policy units (summed policyCount). Federal rule: a lender must require flood insurance on a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area with a federally backed loan (42 U.S.C. §4012a). This is the mix of existing policies, not of all buildings, and does not establish any one property's obligation.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How much does it cost here?

Among existing single-family primary-residence NFIP policies in Jefferson County, the median annual cost is $1,087, with the middle half between $988 and $1,264 (16,640 policies). This is what current policyholders pay — a new policy on a different building can differ.

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus fees), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half (p25–p75); the orange line is FEMA's full-risk price.

Coverage in force: $4,762,609,000 of building and $1,843,129,000 of contents coverage across all Jefferson County policies.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

47.4% of 16,640 single-family policies pay less than FEMA's own full-risk price; the median full-risk premium is $1,237 versus the $1,087 actually charged.

  • Median charged now$1,087
  • Median full-risk price$1,237
  • Pay below full risk47.4% of 16,640

Years to the full-risk price: under the statutory cap, premiums for most primary residences rise at most 18% a year (HFIAA cap, FEMA Risk Rating 2.0). At that maximum rate a policy at today's median ($1,087) would take at least about 1 annual renewals to reach the median full-risk price ($1,237). This is the cap on how fast a bill can climb, not a forecast of any one policy; statutory surcharges and fees are outside the cap.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Can I pay less than the sticker price?

4 of Jefferson County's 10 NFIP communities carry a Community Rating System discount that cuts every eligible policy's premium — up to 15% inside the high-risk zone (Beaumont, City Of).

What do floods actually pay out here?

Between 1978 and 2026, Jefferson County had 22,715 paid NFIP flood claims totalling $1,186,474,726.

Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2017 ($771,842,950), 2019 ($228,274,500), 2008 ($64,551,347). Net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 22,715 paid claims since 1978 against 20,824 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How common is flood insurance here?

Jefferson County has about 19.0 NFIP flood policies for every 100 homes (20,824 policy units vs 109,351 housing units).

  • NFIP policy units20,824
  • Housing units109,351
  • Policies per 100 homes19.0

A coverage-commonness proxy: policy units include some multi-unit and non-residential policies and exclude private flood insurance, so read it as how widespread NFIP coverage is here, not an exact share of households.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP + U.S. Census ACS 5-year 2023 (B25001), retrieved October 22, 2026.

How often is this county a flood disaster?

Jefferson County has had 21 distinct federal flood, hurricane or tropical-storm disaster declarations. The most recent:

  • 2024 — Hurricane: Hurricane Beryl
  • 2020 — Hurricane: Hurricane Laura
  • 2020 — Hurricane: Tropical Storms Marco And Laura
  • 2019 — Flood: Tropical Storm Imelda
  • 2017 — Hurricane: Hurricane Harvey
  • 2008 — Hurricane: Hurricane Ike

Distinct storms by calendar year (one storm's emergency and major-disaster declarations are counted once), not individual declaration records.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective declarations through 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

More data: FEMA disaster aid & reconciliation

Did the government pay homeowners after floods?

FEMA approved $349,138,503 in Individual & Households housing help to Jefferson County homeowners across 8 disasters, on 160,019 valid registrations.

FEMA Individual Assistance is disaster aid, usually capped and partial — separate from NFIP insurance and not a substitute for a policy.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective owner registrations by disaster; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Reconciliation & data completeness

Our counts are checked against FEMA's official figure and the API's own totals.

In-force count: 20,824 policy units (from 20,644 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). FEMA official reconciliation count pending for this county. Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 20644/20644 fetched; claims: 22715/22715 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why premiums are rising — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
